q: Prediction happens in the wild. Where does training happen?
teach: From the lesson: training happens in the workshop, prediction happens in the wild.
teach2: From the lesson: Training happens in the workshop. Prediction happens in the wild. Another way to hold the pair: the long before, in which settings are adjusted over millions of examples, and the quick after, in which one fresh case gets one guess.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson opens by separating the machine's life into two acts. (2) One act adjusts the settings beforehand. (3) The other produces guesses afterwards — training and prediction.

q: What is a prediction, in Professor Kim's plain definition?
answer: a guess about something not yet known
accept: a guess about something not yet known, produced from patterns in things already known
choices: a guess about something not yet known
mcAnswer: a guess about something not yet known
teach: From the lesson: a prediction is the memory of examples, pointed at a new case.
teach2: From the lesson: A prediction is a guess about something not yet known, produced from patterns in things already known. Another way: because it is a guess, it can be wrong; because it comes from patterns, it is usually better than a coin; both halves matter.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson defines the core act part by part. (2) It is a guess, so it can be wrong. (3) And its target is something not yet known.

q: What is inference, in plain words?
accept: the using of the frozen model
teach: From the lesson: inference is the engineer's word for the using of the model.
teach2: From the lesson: Inference is prediction, wearing its work clothes. The pair is worth fixing side by side: training is the showing, inference is the using. Another way: when documentation boasts about inference speed or inference cost, it is boasting about how fast and cheaply the frozen model produces predictions.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Engineers have their own word for running a new case through frozen settings. (2) The lesson translates it on sight. (3) Inference is prediction.

q: In the grading example, the tool's top prediction was right how many times out of twenty enquiries?
teach: From the lesson: count the hits, count the misses, and you have the beginning of knowledge.
teach2: From the lesson: this tool's top prediction was right fourteen times out of twenty. Another way to remember the example: fourteen became clients and six did not, and knowing that split on your own cases is worth more than any brochure.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The tool made its top call on twenty enquiries. (2) The month ended and the outcomes were counted. (3) Fourteen of the twenty became clients — so the answer is fourteen.

q: What is sorting, once you look underneath the decisive way a filter moves a message?
answer: prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off
accept: prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off for display
choices: prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off
mcAnswer: prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off
teach: From the lesson: the filter's decisiveness is a costume.
teach2: From the lesson: Sorting is prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off for display, and once you see that, you will ask the sorter the predictor's question: how often is the sort wrong, and wrong in which direction, because a real enqui Another way: the filter predicted junk was the likely verdict and acted on it — the prediction is still there, with its error rate, under the tidy display.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Sorting looks like knowing because it acts decisively. (2) The lesson looks underneath the act. (3) Underneath is prediction with the uncertainty trimmed off.

q: How does a chatbot produce a paragraph, according to this lesson?
answer: a predictor running in a loop
choices: a predictor running in a loop
mcAnswer: a predictor running in a loop
teach: From the lesson: the maker is a predictor running in a loop.
teach2: From the lesson: predictor running in a loop. It predicts the next word. Then it predicts the next word after that, given the words so far, including its own. Another way: a paragraph is hundreds of small predictions in a row, each shaped by the memory of examples — fluency is what very good, very fast small predictions feel like.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson looks for the prediction inside the maker. (2) It finds the next-word guess. (3) Repeated hundreds of times, that is prediction, in a loop.

q: Why does the lesson say a system usually does not learn from you while you use it?
teach: From the lesson: what feels like learning is prediction with more of your words in the input.
teach2: From the lesson: they do not retrain the model. The settings are frozen. The workshop is elsewhere and elsewhen. Another way: your corrections shape the current conversation because the conversation is part of the input — but the long adjustment happened in the workshop, before the system ever met you.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The timeline separates training from prediction. (2) Your use of the system is all on the prediction side. (3) Nothing retrains because the settings are frozen.

q: Why does prediction work at all, when it works?
teach: From the lesson: a model is a very large collection of the world's habits, distilled into settings.
teach2: From the lesson: Prediction works because the world has habits. People who ask about price in the first line usually keep asking about price. Another way: people who ask about price first usually keep asking about price, and messages shaped like past junk are usually junk — patterns are the fingerprints of those habits.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson asks why guessing from patterns can succeed. (2) It answers with the stability underneath the patterns. (3) Prediction works because the world has habits.

q: What are patterns silent about, however well they predict?
teach: From the lesson: patterns tell you what travels together.
teach2: From the lesson: Patterns tell you what travels together. They are silent about what produces what. Another way: deadline enquiries becoming clients is a pattern worth ranking by — but ordering every client to mention a deadline would manufacture deadlines, not seriousness.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson separates travelling together from causing. (2) Prediction only needs the travelling together. (3) What patterns cannot tell you is what produces what.

q: What is a prediction that is only remembered afterwards, according to the lesson?
accept: not a prediction; it is a story
teach: From the lesson: write it down, date it, count it later.
teach2: From the lesson: A prediction remembered afterwards is not a prediction; it is a story, and stories always grade themselves kindly. Another way: the scoreboard only works when the guess was fixed in writing before the outcome arrived — afterwards, memory edits the guess kindly.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Grading requires the prediction to be recorded in advance. (2) A version recalled after the outcome is not fixed. (3) The lesson calls that a story.

q: In your own words, take one thing a tool does and say what it predicts, from what patterns, about what unknown.
answer: the system predicts this, from patterns in that, about this unknown
choices: the system predicts this, from patterns in that, about this unknown
mcAnswer: the system predicts this, from patterns in that, about this unknown
teach: From the lesson: when you can fill in all three blanks, the tool has no fog left to hide in.
teach2: From the lesson: Run that sentence shape over anything a tool does this week: the system predicts this, from patterns in that, about this unknown. Another way: the draft is a prediction of text, the posting time is a prediction of attention, the summary is a prediction of words — same shape, three blanks, every time.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Name the output as a prediction. (2) Name the patterns it comes from, the memory of examples. (3) Name the unknown it is about — and the tool is translated.
